claims.text: Optimized thermomechanical treatment can refine the grains of coarse-grained eutectic high-entropy alloys.
Thermomechanical grain refinement can simultaneously increase strength and ductility in eutectic high-entropy alloys.
The treatment will produce a refined and uniform grain-size distribution.
The increased grain-boundary area impedes dislocation movement and thereby increases strength.
Grain refinement promotes more uniform deformation and thereby improves ductility.
Relative to the coarse-grained alloy, grain refinement will increase strength by 10–20%.
Relative to the coarse-grained alloy, grain refinement will increase ductility by 15–30%.
The proposed improvement should hold in structural applications having moderate-to-high stress requirements.
Grain sizes below 1 micrometre may diminish the mechanical benefits of refinement.
The diminished benefit below 1 micrometre would result from increased susceptibility to grain-boundary embrittlement.
The grain-size–strength–ductility relationship depends on alloy composition and processing conditions.

contradictions.description: The boundary anticipates diminished benefits when grain size falls below 1 micrometre, but the falsification rule treats a lack of improvement under that same boundary condition as falsifying the hypothesis. An outcome explicitly identified as potentially outside the beneficial regime should not by itself falsify the bounded hypothesis.
